extracted.intended_audience: research community, research-integrity professionals, journalists and general readers interested in scientific misconduct and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and findings used by an institutional investigation to evaluate alleged scientific misconduct in biomedical publications (case: synthetic trachea transplants). Focuses on factual accuracy, ethical approvals/consents, preclinical work, and individual author responsibility and retraction recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated and distorted descriptions of patients' conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The articles contain fabricated and distorted descriptions of the patients’ conditions before and after the operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious inaccuracies and misleading information in case descriptions constitute grounds for finding misconduct; such fabrication/distortion undermines the validity of reported outcomes and patient selection claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of justification for treatment on grounds of 'vital indication'
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification is lacking for treatment of the patients on the grounds of so-called vital indication (when a given treatment is the last resort for survival).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authors claim a treatment was performed as a last-resort 'vital indication', investigators should expect clear, documented justification; absent or weak justification suggests inappropriate clinical decision-making and may indicate misconduct if misrepresented in publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to reference or perform required preclinical (animal) experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: One [article] misses reference to relevant animal experiments which must precede human studies that involve unproven methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human studies of unproven methods require prior and properly reported preclinical work (e.g., animal experiments); omission of such references or absence of requisite preclinical research is a serious procedural and ethical lapse and may be treated as misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of ethical approvals
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical research involving patients must have documented approvals from appropriate ethical review boards; publishing clinical interventions without such approvals is a major breach and a basis for retraction or misconduct findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of appropriate informed consents
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers must obtain and document informed consent from human subjects when required; failure to secure appropriate consent undermines ethical validity of the study and supports misconduct or retraction actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors bear individual responsibility for inaccuracies regardless of whistleblowing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is KI’s firm opinion that a whistle blower who has participated in a scientific study and also as author of a scientific article, despite reporting, cannot be freed from blame or absolved from responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may hold each listed author responsible for content they helped produce even if they later raised concerns; investigations may therefore evaluate co-authors individually and not treat whistleblowing as blanket exculpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to retract articles containing serious inaccuracies and ethical lapses
rubrics_metrics.description: KI is also calling to retract six articles ... The investigation uncovered 'serious inaccuracies and misleading information' and notes missing ethical approvals and consents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publications are found to contain fabricated or distorted patient descriptions, lack necessary ethical approvals/consents, or omit required preclinical evidence, the institution may recommend journal retraction without undue delay; journals may also issue expressions of concern while evaluating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized assessment of each author's responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Karolinska Institutet’s investigation has examined the responsibility of each individual author (a total of 43 researchers). According to the President’s decision, an additional 31 authors are blameworthy for their contributions ... another five authors are cleared of blame and of responsibility for scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations may assign differing outcomes to authors (responsible for misconduct, blameworthy but not guilty of misconduct, cleared); thorough inquiries examine each author's contribution and culpability rather than treating all co-authors identically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrepancy between investigative bodies' assignment of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Today’s decision differs from the report of the Expert group for misconduct in research at the Central Ethical Review Board, CEPN, who considers all authors responsible for scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different oversight or review bodies may reach divergent conclusions about authors' responsibility; institutional findings and central ethical board findings can differ in scope and attribution of blame, which affects retraction requests and public communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals' interim actions (expressions of concern) pending investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lancet paper has already been flagged with an expression of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may flag suspect articles with expressions of concern while investigations proceed; such flags signal potential problems and are part of the remediation toolkit prior to retraction decisions.
